cohort: Regular English-taught September 2026 entrant, standard full-time route.

courseDetails.entry: You are enrolled as a student of the Bachelor's programme Computational Social Science, or you are an exchange student.
courseDetails.contents: The major part of the semester is organised around two project challenges (themes: climate change and surveillance). You will be introduced to design thinking and learn how to search, collect, close read, summarise and reference scientific literature. You will also take workshops on peer collaboration, time management, feedback, and reflection.Additionally, you will study theories that help you conceptualise the complexity of social challenges and the tension between structure and agency. You will acquire a basic ability to identify stakeholders and explore their perspectives and interests. You will acquire knowledge and insight into various digital interventions at different levels of analysis, and learn how these interventions may both alleviate and aggravate the problems at hand. Finally, you will acquire basic insights in the governance of digitisation and underlying normative questions. You are introduced to the empirical cycle and will practice with interviews, surveys, and related techniques for data analysis. The basics of computational thinking are also introduced, and you will start to develop programming skills in Python. You will work on your own survey data to develop skills in data wrangling and data visualisation. Lastly, you will reflect on your group project and deliverables, your individual contribution and learning objectives.

courseDetails.entry: You are enrolled as a student of the Bachelor's programme Computational Social Science and have completed and obtained credits for the course 'Foundation: Appreciating the Complexity of Social Challenges' (Year 1, Semester 1)
courseDetails.priorKnowledge: Knowledge and skills acquired in the course 'Foundation: Appreciating the Complexity of Social Challenges' (Year 1, Semester 1)
courseDetails.contents: The semester revolves around developing a prototype of a digital behavioural change intervention addressing a societal issue related to sustainability, surveillance, mobility, or health. You will go through three design cycles, developing your prototype with input from your research, project partner, and lecturers. This project work lasts approximately 16 weeks and includes (a) focus groups to explore opportunities and obstacles for individual behaviour and for the adoption of tools, (b) building a website prototype of a digital intervention, (c) adding new ideas to your prototype through desk research, and (d) conducting a pilot experiment to test these ideas.While doing so, you will learn, practice, and reflect on collaboration, personal traits, professional ethics, and persuasive writing and design. You will gain theoretical insights into individual-level antecedents and social structures, study specific theories and empirical research on behavioural change, and conduct a literature review on a case of your choice. Furthermore, you will learn how to create basic websites and database structures, continuing your training in programming skills.

courseDetails.entry: You are enrolled as a student of the Bachelor's programme Computational Social Science. You must also have completed and obtained credits for the course 'Foundation: Appreciating the Complexity of Social Challenges' (Year 1, Semester 1) and have completed the course 'Building Blocks: Experimenting with digital interventions for behavioural change' (Year 1, Semester 2).
courseDetails.priorKnowledge: Knowledge and skills acquired in the courses 'Foundation: Appreciating the Complexity of Social Challenges' (Year 1, Semester 1) and 'Building Blocks: Experimenting with digital interventions for behavioural change' (Year 1, Semester 2).
courseDetails.contents: You will be challenged to think about (systemic) digital interventions that may improve the interaction, coordination or communication between stakeholders in a mobility system or a health system. You will work in project teams on challenges proposed by external partners. Given that systemic digital interventions are inherently complex, your final deliverable will be an intervention document to develop or implement a digital intervention, rather than a digital technology itself. In this intervention document, you will pay attention to relevant policy-related and normative considerations, as well as the need for theoretical grounding and the application of appropriate methods.To this end, you will learn new methods for digital data collection and analysis, such as natural language processing (NLP), agent-based modelling (ABM), social network analysis (SNA), as well as unsupervised and supervised machine learning.To facilitate your project work, you will learn about complex processes and system thinking and study theoretical, empirical and non-scientific literature on social practices and systems that are relevant to your project group's research question. Lastly, you will reflect on your group project and deliverables, your individual contribution and learning objectives.

courseDetails.entry: You are enrolled as a student of the Bachelor's programme Computational Social Science. You must also have completed and obtained credits for the courses 'Foundation' (Year 1, Semester 1), 'Building Blocks' (Year 1, Semester 2) and 'Connections' (Year 2, Semester 3).
courseDetails.priorKnowledge: Knowledge and skills acquired in the courses 'Foundation: Appreciating the Complexity of Social Challenges' (Year 1, Semester 1), 'Building Blocks: Experimenting with digital interventions for behavioural change' (Year 1, Semester 2) and 'Connections: Linking data for better interventions in health or mobility systems' (Year 2, Semester 3).
courseDetails.contents: You will work in a project group to create or contribute to the creation of a predictive model using curent, real-world data. You will go through every step of the data science lifecycle. You will reflect on the implications, assumptions and consequences of the decisions and choices you need to make. You will engage with stakeholders that are affected by biased algorithmic decision-making, and with communities that try to correct these biases.You will reflect on why algorithms would need to be applied to a certain social process at all, and on the implications of datafication in that case. And you will conduct a scenario study, in which you explore possible trend reversals and unpredictable events that may impact your predictions. This should all contribute to the final deliverable, which is a presentation demonstrating a responsible algorithmic decision-making system. The presentation and demo should be supported by a report and a critical reflection about the risks for bias as well as implications for individuals, groups and society at large. Lastly, you will reflect on your group project and deliverables, your individual contribution and learning objectives.

courseDetails.priorKnowledge: Knowledge and skills acquired in the courses 'Foundation: Appreciating the Complexity of Social Challenges' (Year 1, Semester 1), 'Building Blocks: Experimenting with digital interventions for behavioural change' (Year 1, Semester 2), 'Connections: Linking data for better interventions in health or mobility systems' (Year 2, Semester 3) and 'STRUCTURES: Applying responsible AI to reduce inequality' (Year 2, Semester 4) as part of the Computational Social Science BSc programme.
courseDetails.contents: You will be challenged to think about interventions for social change. You will work in project teams on challenges proposed by external partners and develop and implement an intervention. By employing both social science and data science techniques for data gathering and analysis, you will craft and execute an intervention. Through regular meetings with your Core Lecturer and Project Partner, you will consistently evaluate the progress of your project work. You will have intermediary presentations and evaluation points to keep you on track. Your final deliverables will be a research report and the digital intervention.

components: Foundation: Appreciating the complexity of social challenges
Building blocks: Experimenting with digital interventions for behavioural change
Connections: Linking data for better interventions in health or mobility systems
Structures: Applying responsible AI to reduce inequality
Electives, minor, internship or study abroad
Capstone: Making social change with digital innovations
progression: 60 EC per year, consisting of five separately credited semester modules and a 30 EC elective semester. The knowledge strands and project products are embedded in those modules. The programme has no named route choice; health and mobility are project contexts inside Connections.

The first four modules are taken in order. The dated catalogue gives earlier cumulative entry conditions for Connections and Structures, all satisfied on this plan. The capstone catalogue leaves its entry text blank, so Article B.4.5 supplies the requirement to pass Structures. Electives take place in the first semester of year three and remain choice space under Article B.4.3.a. No internship is compulsory.
Connections is a partner challenge whose output is an intervention document. The capstone requires partner-based implementation and a research report. Its group research is included within its 30 EC.
